title: How Often Should an HVAC System Be Serviced?
h1: How Often Should You Service Your HVAC System?
description: Most homes should have the HVAC system serviced once a year, and twice for heat pumps or heavy use. Learn what a tune-up covers and the best time to book.
quick_answer: Have your HVAC system professionally serviced at least once a year. Homes with a heat pump, which heats and cools from the same equipment, or with heavy summer AC use benefit from two visits: one in spring before cooling season and one in fall before the heat comes on. Between visits, check the filter monthly and keep the outdoor unit clear.
body:
Why does yearly service matter?

Heating and cooling equipment wears gradually. Capacitors weaken, flame sensors get coated, drain lines collect sludge and coils gather dust. None of that is dramatic on day one, but it adds up to higher bills, uneven comfort and a breakdown on the first heat wave or cold snap of the season.

A tune-up catches these small issues while they're cheap to fix. It also gives a technician a chance to check safety items, like the furnace heat exchanger and gas connections, that most homeowners can't inspect themselves.

Is once a year enough, or should it be twice?

It depends on the equipment and how hard it works:

  • Gas furnace with central AC. One visit a year can work, but splitting it into a spring AC check and a fall furnace check is better if you use both.
  • Heat pump. Twice a year. The same outdoor unit runs in both seasons, so it gets more hours of wear.
  • Ductless mini-splits. At least once a year, with indoor filter cleaning every month or two.
  • Light-use coastal homes. Once a year is usually fine if the system only runs on cold nights and a few warm days.
  • Inland homes with long cooling seasons. A spring AC tune-up before summer is a must.

When is the best time to schedule?

Spring is ideal for air conditioning. Booking before inland temperatures climb means you're not waiting in line on the first hot weekend. Fall is ideal for heating, ahead of the cold nights that settle in from November through February.

If you only book one visit, choose the season your system works hardest. For most inland homes that's spring. For many coastal homes that rarely use AC, fall makes more sense.

What does an HVAC tune-up include?

A proper maintenance visit should go well beyond a quick look. Expect the technician to:

  1. Check and replace or clean the air filter
  2. Test thermostat operation and calibration
  3. Inspect and tighten electrical connections, and test capacitors and contactors
  4. Clean the flame sensor and check the igniter and burners on gas furnaces
  5. Inspect the heat exchanger area and venting for signs of problems
  6. Check refrigerant pressures and temperature split on cooling equipment
  7. Rinse the outdoor condenser coil and clear debris
  8. Flush the condensate drain line and check the drain pan
  9. Check blower operation and airflow

You should get a short written summary of what was checked and anything that needs attention. Our HVAC tune-up and repair service covers each of these steps.

What can you do between service visits?

Homeowners can handle a few simple tasks that make a real difference:

  • Check the filter every month and change it when it's dirty
  • Keep two feet of clear space around the outdoor unit
  • Rinse salt residue off coastal outdoor units with a gentle hose spray now and then
  • Keep supply vents and return grilles open and unblocked by furniture
  • Test carbon monoxide alarms and replace their batteries

Leave gas valves, refrigerant and electrical internals to a technician. If you ever smell gas, leave the house and call the gas utility from outside. If a carbon monoxide alarm sounds, get everyone out and call 911.

What happens if you skip maintenance?

Skipping a year usually won't cause an immediate breakdown, but small problems compound. A dirty coil makes the compressor run hotter. A weak capacitor strains the motor it starts. A clogged drain line can overflow into a ceiling, especially when the air handler is in the attic.

Many equipment manufacturers also expect regular professional maintenance as part of their warranty terms, so keep your service records. Check the specials page for current tune-up offers.

Do coastal and inland homes need different maintenance?

The checklist is the same, but the focus shifts. Near the coast, salt air corrodes outdoor coil fins and electrical connections, so technicians pay close attention to rust and give the condenser a good rinse. Damp air also makes clean drain lines more important.

Inland, the outdoor unit works much harder through long, hot summers and collects more dust and dry leaves. Coil cleaning, capacitor testing and refrigerant checks before summer matter most there. Homes in fire-prone areas should also expect a filter change after any smoke event.
faqs: Do new HVAC systems need yearly service?

Yes. New equipment still collects dust, and the first couple of years are when installation issues like refrigerant charge or drainage problems tend to show up. Keeping up with maintenance also helps protect the manufacturer's warranty.
How long does an HVAC tune-up take?
Most tune-ups take about an hour per system. Homes with more than one system, or equipment in a tight attic, may take a bit longer.
Can I service my own HVAC system?
You can change filters, clear debris from the outdoor unit and keep vents open. Testing electrical parts, checking refrigerant and inspecting gas components should be done by a trained technician.
Is fall or spring better for HVAC service?
Spring is best for air conditioning and heat pumps before summer. Fall is best for furnaces before the cold nights. If you book only one visit, pick the season your system works hardest.
